pages.name: A charged cell
pages.text: A lead-acid cell is two plates standing in sulphuric acid. On the left is the positive plate, made of lead dioxide. On the right is the negative plate, made of plain lead. Between them, the acid is mixed with water. Together they are the cell's [[electrolyte]]. Each dot stands for a little of the acid. A terminal on top of each plate carries the current in and out. The gauge below shows how strong the acid is. This cell is fully charged.

pages.name: A lamp
pages.task: The lamp switch is closed, so the cell starts to discharge. Before you see it, predict: what do the two plates turn into?
pages.why: Each plate reacts with the acid where they meet. At the lead plate, lead and acid make lead sulphate. At the lead dioxide plate, lead dioxide and acid make lead sulphate too. Nothing travels from plate to plate. Both turn into the same substance where they stand.

pages.name: Charge running down
pages.text: As the cell discharges, both plates turn into the same white substance, [[lead sulphate]]. Each plate reacts with the acid where they meet. The acid is used up to make the sulphate, so acid dots leave the liquid for the plates. The gauge shows the acid getting weaker. At half charge, both plates are part white. At flat, the plates are mostly lead sulphate, and the acid is weak but not yet water.

pages.name: The acid
pages.task: The cell runs from full right down to flat. What happens to the strength of its acid?
pages.why: The acid is not just a bath for the plates. It is one of the things being used up to make lead sulphate. So its strength falls as the cell discharges. A flat cell still holds some weak acid, so it stops short of water.

pages.name: Round the wire
pages.text: With the lamp switch closed, current flows. Electrons freed at the lead plate cannot cross the acid. They run round the outside wire, through the lamp, to the lead dioxide plate. Conventional current, the way you draw it, runs the other way. Inside the liquid, [[ions]] carry the current. Ions are the acid's charged pieces. Positive ones drift towards the lead dioxide plate, negative ones towards the lead plate. With both switches open, only a slow self-discharge goes on. Here the lamp is lit, and the charge falls.

pages.name: Through the acid
pages.task: Electrons carry the current round the outside wire. What carries it through the acid?
pages.why: Electrons cannot cross the acid. One plate gives out electrons and the other takes them in. Left alone, charge would pile up beside each plate. The acid's ions drift and keep it balanced, and that closes the loop. No ion carries an electron across.

pages.name: Charging
pages.text: A charger runs the whole thing backwards. It pushes current in against the cell's own push, so it needs a higher voltage than the cell. Electrons and ions now run the other way. The lead sulphate turns back into lead on one plate and lead dioxide on the other. The acid locked in the sulphate returns to the liquid, so the acid gets stronger. That makes it a [[secondary cell]], one you can recharge. A torch battery is a primary cell, used once. Here the cell is fully charged again.

pages.name: What charging does
pages.task: A charger is now across a flat cell. What does charging do?
pages.answer: Turns the sulphate back and strengthens the acid
pages.why: Charging runs the whole thing backwards. The lead sulphate turns back into lead dioxide on one plate and lead on the other. The acid locked in the sulphate returns to the liquid, so the acid gets stronger.

pages.name: Two plates, two voltages
pages.text: The cell's push comes from its two plates. Each plate has its own voltage, set mainly by what it is made of. Both are read against the same reference electrode, like two points read from one 0 V rail. Lead dioxide sits at +1.685 V and lead at −0.356 V. The cell's voltage is the gap between them, 2.04 V. The rail drops out of that difference. A charged cell's acid is stronger than standard, so it rests a little higher, at about 2.1 V.

pages.name: The gap
pages.task: Lead dioxide sits at +1.685 V and lead at −0.356 V. What is the gap between them?
pages.why: Lead sits 0.356 V below the reference, and lead dioxide 1.685 V above it. So the gap is 1.685 + 0.356 = 2.04 V. That gap is the cell's voltage for acid of a standard strength.

pages.name: Bigger plates, more cells
pages.text: Plate size is not in that sum. A bigger plate holds more material to turn into lead sulphate. So it gives more ampere-hours at the same volts. Here the plates are four times the size, so the example cell gives 400 Ah instead of 100 Ah. Its voltmeter still reads 2.1 V. For more volts, put cells in series. Twelve cells make a 24 V battery. Charged and rested, it reads about 25.2 V.

pages.why: The volts come from the plate materials, lead dioxide and lead in the same acid. Size is not in that sum, so both read about 2.1 V. The big cell holds more plate material, so it gives more ampere-hours.

pages.name: A 24 V battery
pages.task: A ship's emergency battery of lead-acid cells is marked 24 V. How many cells has it, and what does it read charged and rested?
pages.why: Each cell is 2 V nominal, so 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cells in series. Charged and rested, each reads about 2.1 V. So the battery reads about 12 × 2.1 = 25.2 V.
